_note: Fictional sources for teaching: every source cited here is invented. See sources.json.
title: The shopping list
context: A politics student is writing about social media and young people's political engagement.
question: What is the main problem with this paragraph?
text: Social media has changed how young people engage with politics, and researchers have studied this in several ways. {{cite:abara2017|integral}} found that young adults who used social media every day were more interested in politics than those who did not. {{cite:delacourt2019|integral}} found that many people share political posts without reading beyond the headline. {{cite:quigley2022|integral}} found that online political activity was only weakly linked to voting in national elections. These studies all show that social media is important for politics. There are many different views on social media and politics, and more research is needed in this area before firm conclusions can be drawn.

problems.text: The sources are listed one per sentence, but never connected to each other or to a point.
problems.feedback: Yes. Each source gets its own sentence starting '[Author] found that…', and the writer never says how the findings relate. In fact they pull in different directions — and that tension is the most interesting thing here.
Three sources is plenty for one paragraph. The problem is what the paragraph does with them.

problems.text: The citations should all be grouped together at the end of the paragraph.
problems.feedback: That would make things worse: the reader couldn't tell which finding came from which source. Grouping citations is fine when several sources make the same point — not when they make different ones.

problems.text: Each finding should be a direct quotation.
problems.feedback: In the social sciences, summarising findings in your own words is usually better. Quotations wouldn't fix the main problem.

repaired: [[c1:Social media appears to raise young people's interest in politics more than their participation in it.]] [[c2:Daily users report greater political interest than non-users {{cite:abara2017}}, but interest does not seem to translate reliably into action: online political activity is only weakly linked to voting in national elections {{cite:quigley2022}}.]] [[c3:One reason may be the shallowness of much online engagement, since many people share political posts without reading beyond the headline {{cite:delacourt2019}}.]] [[c4:If so, counting likes and shares may overstate how politically active young people really are, and researchers interested in participation would do better to measure what users do offline.]]

annotations.c1: The paragraph now starts with the writer's own claim, which the sources are organised around.
annotations.c2: Two sources are set against each other with 'but'. The connection between them is the point.
annotations.c3: The third source is offered as a possible explanation — and hedged ('may'), because it doesn't prove the link.
annotations.c4: The writer's own conclusion, which none of the sources states on its own.

notes.text: Numeric styles number sources in the order they first appear. Because the repaired paragraph discusses the sources in a different order, the numbers change — the reference list follows the paragraph.
In the flawed version, each author is named in the writer's sentence, so MLA gives the full name at first mention. The repaired version cites in brackets, which in MLA use the surname only.

chefsNote: Three sources in three sentences is a shopping list, not a sauce.
